review_flags: Dimensionality claim: the page says Word2Vec and Transformers have similar embedding sizes, 'somewhere between 1,000 and 10,000 dimensions'. The published Word2Vec vectors (Mikolov et al., 2013, Google News model) are 300-dimensional, and the original experiments mostly used 50-1,000 dimensions. The RoBERTa base model the chapter itself fine-tunes (pp.479-485) has a hidden size of 768. Only very large LLMs reach a few thousand to about 12,000. The range is wrong for Word2Vec and for the chapter's own model.

overview.title: From Word2Vec's word arithmetic to attention as embedding refinement
overview.main_topic: Why Transformers work: the Word2Vec analogy, the 'gender vector' (V(king) - V(man) + V(woman) = V(queen)), and attention as a mechanism that turns token co-occurrence into embedding proximity, giving semantically continuous and interpolative spaces
overview.central_idea: Large Transformers and the humble Word2Vec rest on the same principle: tokens that occur together end up close in a vector space. Attention is what connects the Transformer's next-word loss to that principle. It builds each new embedding space by recombining the previous one, weighting tokens by their dot-product closeness, and so produces spaces that are semantically continuous and interpolative.
overview.importance: This is the book's conceptual explanation of why the Transformer architecture built in 15.3 (pp.461-477) is so effective. It recasts attention as a geometric operation on embedding spaces rather than an engineering trick. That view supports the 'database of vector programs' and 'interpolation and hallucination' claims on pp.487-488, and it frames the LLMs of chapter 16.
learning_objectives: Describe Word2Vec's training objective: turn co-occurrence into dot-product (cosine) proximity
Explain 'word arithmetic' and the gender vector V(king) - V(man) + V(woman) ≈ V(queen)
List the similarities the authors draw between Word2Vec and Transformers (token embeddings, co-occurrence principle, cosine distance, dimensionality)
Explain how attention links a language-modeling loss to the goal of grouping co-occurring tokens
Describe a Transformer as a stack of incrementally refined embedding spaces
Define semantic continuity and semantic interpolation in an embedding space
prerequisites: Word embeddings and meaningful directions in embedding space (pp.433-434)
Dot product and cosine similarity of vectors

summary:
The page continues the Word2Vec story begun on p.485. In 2013 Tomas Mikolov and colleagues at Google trained an embedding in which the dot-product (cosine proximity) of vectors for frequently co-occurring words was pushed **toward 1**, and for rarely co-occurring words **toward 0**.

The resulting space did more than capture similarity. It showed an emergent **"word arithmetic"**: one vector, a **gender vector**, could be added to many male nouns to land near their female equivalents, as in `V(king) - V(man) + V(woman) = V(queen)`. Nobody trained the model for this. There seemed to be dozens of such **magic vectors**: a plural vector, a wild-animal-to-pet vector, and so on.

About ten years later, large pretrained Transformers produce fluent text and seem knowledgeable about almost anything, which Word2Vec never could. Yet the authors argue they share Word2Vec's core: both **embed tokens in a vector space**; both learn that space on the principle that **tokens appearing together end up close**; both compare tokens with **cosine distance**; and the authors put both at roughly **1,000-10,000 dimensions** (a figure that does not hold for Word2Vec; see the review flag).

The obvious objection: a Transformer is trained to predict missing words, not to group tokens. The answer is **attention**, "by far, the most critical component". Attention learns a new token embedding space by **linearly recombining** embeddings from a prior space, weighting tokens that are already close (higher dot-product) more heavily. Over time this pulls close tokens closer, so **correlation relationships become proximity relationships**. A Transformer is a **series of incrementally refined embedding spaces**, each built from the previous one.

Attention gives two properties. The learned spaces are **semantically continuous**: a small move in the space changes meaning only a little (Word2Vec had this too). They are also **semantically interpolative**: the midpoint between two points represents an "intermediate meaning". That sentence continues on p.487.

paragraphs.excerpt: be closer to 1, while the dot-product between vectors representing rarely
paragraphs.what_it_says: This finishes the sentence from p.485 about Word2Vec's objective. Vectors of frequently co-occurring words should have a dot-product near 1, and vectors of rarely co-occurring words a dot-product near 0.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Word2Vec turns a statistical fact (two words often appear near each other) into a geometric one (their vectors point the same way). Co-occurrence counts become angles.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: The rest of the section argues that Transformers do the same thing, only much more powerfully. This objective is the baseline for that comparison.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: in skip-gram with negative sampling, the model scores a (word, context) pair as $\sigma(\mathbf{u}_w\cdot\mathbf{v}_c)$. Training pushes that probability toward 1 for observed pairs and toward 0 for randomly sampled ones. The raw dot-product is unbounded, so 'closer to 1 / 0' is best read as the sigmoid of the dot-product, or as cosine similarity after normalization.

terminology.meaning: A family of shallow embedding models (skip-gram and CBOW) from Mikolov et al., 2013, that learn word vectors from co-occurrence in a text window.
Two words appearing within the same small context window.

connections: p.485: the sentence begins with Mikolov's 2013 Word2Vec work and its similarity to the CBOW model
p.440: the book's own CBOW model predicts a middle word from the average embedding of its neighbours

paragraphs.excerpt: They found that the resulting embedding space did much more than capture
paragraphs.what_it_says: The Word2Vec space showed emergent 'word arithmetic'. A single vector could be added to many male nouns to land near their female equivalents: V(king) - V(man) + V(woman) = V(queen). The model was never trained for this, and there seemed to be dozens of such 'magic vectors' (plural, wild animal to pet, and others).
paragraphs.what_it_means: Semantic relations such as gender or number are encoded as roughly constant offsets, that is, directions in the space. Because the offset is the same for many word pairs, it works like a function, `female(x) ≈ x + g`.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the first concrete case of a model learning useful 'functions' as a by-product of organizing tokens geometrically. On p.487 the authors scale the idea up into 'vector programs' inside Transformers.
paragraphs.technical_idea: In practice the result is found by nearest-neighbour search. Compute $\mathbf{t}=V(\text{king})-V(\text{man})+V(\text{woman})$, then return the vocabulary word with the highest cosine similarity to $\mathbf{t}$, excluding the three input words. The '=' in the book stands for 'is nearest to'.

terminology.meaning: Adding and subtracting word vectors to perform analogies.
The offset V(woman) - V(man), roughly shared by many male/female word pairs.
A capability that appears without being an explicit training target.

connections: p.434: figure 14.4's toy space has a 'from pet to wild animal' vector and a 'from canine to feline' vector; real spaces have gender and plural vectors

paragraphs.excerpt: Fast-forward about 10 years—we are now in the age of large, pretrained
paragraphs.what_it_says: Today's large pretrained Transformers look nothing like Word2Vec on the surface. They generate fluent language, which Word2Vec could not do at all, and (as chapter 16 will show) they seem knowledgeable about almost any topic. Yet they have a lot in common with Word2Vec.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The authors set up a thesis: the impressive surface behaviour hides a simple, shared mechanism.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It frames the rest of the section as demystification. Fluency should not be read as evidence of a fundamentally different kind of system.

terminology.meaning: A Transformer first trained on a large unlabeled corpus with a language-modeling objective, then reused (as RoBERTa was on pp.479-485).

connections: p.490: chapter 16 opens on text generation with large pretrained models

paragraphs.excerpt: Both models seek to embed tokens (words or subwords) in a vector space
paragraphs.what_it_says: Four similarities: (1) both embed tokens, words or subwords, in a vector space; (2) both learn it on the principle that tokens appearing together end up close; (3) both compare tokens with cosine distance; (4) both use similar dimensionality, 'between 1,000 and 10,000 dimensions'.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The authors claim a family resemblance at the level of representation. Both are maps from tokens to points in which closeness reflects co-occurrence.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: These shared features justify reading Transformer behaviour through the Word2Vec lens for the rest of the section.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Note (not in the book): the dimensionality figure is inaccurate (see the review flag). Common Word2Vec vectors have 300 dimensions, and RoBERTa base, used on pp.479-485, has 768. Also, Transformers compute raw scaled dot-products in attention rather than normalized cosines. Cosine is the usual way to *analyze* both spaces.

terminology.meaning: $1-\cos\theta$, where $\cos\theta = \frac{\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}}{\|\mathbf{a}\|\|\mathbf{b}\|}$. It depends only on direction, not length.
A token smaller than a word, such as a byte-pair-encoding piece, used by modern tokenizers.

connections: p.433: geometric distance (cosine or L2) between word vectors should reflect semantic distance

paragraphs.excerpt: At this point, you might interject: A Transformer is trained to predict
paragraphs.what_it_says: The objection: a Transformer is trained to predict missing words, not to group tokens in a space. How does a language-model loss relate to Word2Vec's goal of maximizing the dot-product between co-occurring tokens? The answer is the attention mechanism.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The training *objective* is different, but the *architecture* contains a component that does the grouping. Attention, used in service of next-token prediction, ends up organizing the space by co-occurrence.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This sets up the main claim of the section: attention is the bridge between 'predict tokens' and 'build a meaningful geometry'.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: Word2Vec itself is also a prediction task (predict context words, or the middle word in CBOW). The similarity of the two objectives is closer than the objection suggests. Both are 'predict a token from its neighbours', and the Transformer does it with a deep, context-dependent model.

terminology.meaning: Cross-entropy of the predicted distribution over the next (or masked) token, p(token|past tokens) or p(token|surrounding tokens).

connections: p.479: masked language modeling, p(token|surrounding tokens), used to pretrain BERT/RoBERTa

paragraphs.excerpt: Attention is, by far, the most critical component in the Transformer architecture
paragraphs.what_it_says: Attention learns a new token embedding space by linearly recombining token embeddings from a prior space. The weights favour tokens that are already 'closer', meaning they have a higher dot-product. This pulls close vectors together, until correlation relationships become proximity (cosine) relationships. Transformers learn a series of incrementally refined embedding spaces, each built by recombining the previous one. The paragraph ends: 'Attention provides Transformers with two crucial properties:'.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Each output vector is a weighted average of input vectors, with weights given by similarity. Averaging similar vectors makes them more alike (a 'rich get closer' dynamic). Stacking layers repeats the process on ever more contextual representations.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It turns the equations of 15.3.1 (p.463) into a geometric picture: attention is a similarity-weighted smoothing of the token cloud, and depth gives progressively refined maps.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: in formula form, $\mathbf{y}_i=\sum_j \alpha_{ij}\,\mathbf{v}_j$ with $\alpha_{ij}=\operatorname{softmax}_j(\mathbf{q}_i\cdot\mathbf{k}_j/\sqrt{d})$. The output is a convex combination of value vectors, so it always lies inside their convex hull. This is why 'recombination' and 'interpolation' are apt descriptions of a single attention step. Residual connections and feedforward layers then add nonlinear refinements.

terminology.meaning: An operation that computes each token's new vector as a softmax-weighted sum of (projected) vectors of all tokens, with weights from dot-product scores.
The output of each Transformer block, which serves as a new representation space for the next block.

connections: p.463: dot-product attention (15.3.1) defines the score-softmax-weighted-sum computation
p.488: the chapter summary repeats that vectors near each other are summed together in attention

paragraphs.excerpt: The embedding spaces they learn are semantically continuous—that is, moving a
paragraphs.what_it_says: Property 1: the learned spaces are semantically continuous. Moving a little in the space changes the human-facing meaning only a little. Word2Vec's space had this property too.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Meaning is a smooth function of position. There are no cliffs where a tiny perturbation flips 'cat' into 'bankruptcy'. Nearby points mean nearby things.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Continuity is what makes gradient-based learning and generalization possible: unseen inputs near seen ones get similar treatment. On p.487 it becomes the 'move around on the curve' property of the Transformer-as-database.

terminology.meaning: Small distances in embedding space correspond to small differences in meaning.

connections: p.487: you can move around on the curve to explore nearby, related points

paragraphs.excerpt: The embedding spaces they learn are semantically interpolative—that is, taking the
paragraphs.what_it_says: Property 2: the spaces are semantically interpolative. The intermediate point between two embeddings represents the 'intermediate meaning' between the corresponding tokens. The sentence finishes on p.487, which explains that each space is built by interpolating between vectors of the previous one.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Not only are neighbourhoods meaningful. Straight-line paths between meanings also pass through meaningful territory.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Interpolation is the basis of the authors' later claims that Transformers can 'retrieve more than you put in', which gives generalization but also hallucination (p.487). It also underlies their view that these models are 'fundamentally interpolative' (p.488).
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: interpolation means $\mathbf{z}(t)=(1-t)\,\mathbf{a}+t\,\mathbf{b}$ for $t\in[0,1]$. Since attention outputs are convex combinations of value vectors, they are literally interpolations of the previous layer's (projected) vectors.

terminology.meaning: Points between two embeddings decode to meanings between the two endpoints.

connections: p.487: continuation, 'This comes from the fact that each new embedding space is built by interpolating…'

concepts.name: Word / token embedding space
concepts.definition: A mapping from each token to a dense vector, learned so that geometric relationships reflect semantic or co-occurrence relationships.
concepts.intuition: A map of meaning where related words are neighbours and consistent relations are consistent directions.
concepts.technical: Word2Vec learns one static vector per word with a shallow model. A Transformer starts from a static embedding table and then produces a new, context-dependent embedding at every layer.
concepts.significance: The authors' unifying lens for Word2Vec and Transformers on this page.
concepts.example: Vectors for 'movie' and 'film' should be nearly identical (p.433).
concepts.misconception: That an embedding's individual coordinates are interpretable features. Meaning lives in relative directions and distances, not in single axes.

concepts.name: Word arithmetic / magic vectors
concepts.definition: The emergent property that semantic relations are approximately constant vector offsets, so analogies can be solved by vector addition and subtraction.
concepts.intuition: The step from 'man' to 'woman' is the same arrow as the step from 'king' to 'queen'.
concepts.technical: Solve a:b :: c:? by computing $V(b)-V(a)+V(c)$ and returning the nearest word by cosine, excluding a, b and c.
concepts.significance: It shows that geometry learned from co-occurrence alone can encode functions. This is the seed of the 'vector programs' idea on p.487.
concepts.example: V(king) - V(man) + V(woman) ≈ V(queen) (gender vector); a plural vector maps cat to cats.
concepts.misconception: That the equation holds exactly. It is a nearest-neighbour approximation, and it works much better for some relations than others.

concepts.name: Attention as embedding refinement
concepts.definition: The authors' interpretation of attention: it learns a new embedding space by linearly recombining the previous space's token vectors, weighted toward tokens that are already close (higher dot-product).
concepts.intuition: Every token takes a similarity-weighted average of the crowd around it, so similar tokens drift together.
concepts.technical: $\mathbf{y}_i = \sum_j \operatorname{softmax}_j(\mathbf{q}_i\cdot\mathbf{k}_j/\sqrt{d})\,\mathbf{v}_j$. The output is a convex combination of value vectors. Stacked blocks give a sequence of refined spaces.
concepts.significance: The authors call it 'by far, the most critical component' of the Transformer. It explains how a next-token loss produces co-occurrence geometry.
concepts.example: In 'the bank of the river', the vector for 'bank' gets mixed with 'river', moving it toward the geographic sense.
concepts.misconception: That attention is just a lookup or a hard selection. Softmax produces a soft, weighted blend of all tokens.

concepts.name: Semantic continuity
concepts.definition: Moving a small distance in the embedding space changes the human-facing meaning only slightly.
concepts.intuition: There are no sudden jumps in meaning; nearby points mean nearby things.
concepts.technical: Roughly, meaning is a Lipschitz-like function of position near the data manifold.
concepts.significance: It enables generalization to inputs near the training data and exploration of related ideas (p.487).
concepts.example: Nudging the vector for 'warm' slightly toward 'hot' produces something like 'very warm', not an unrelated word.
concepts.misconception: That continuity holds everywhere in the space. It holds near regions supported by data; far off the manifold, points may decode to nonsense.

concepts.name: Semantic interpolation
concepts.definition: The point between two embeddings represents an intermediate meaning between the two tokens.
concepts.intuition: Halfway between 'cat' and 'tiger' sits something like 'wild cat'.
concepts.technical: $\mathbf{z}(t)=(1-t)\mathbf{a}+t\mathbf{b}$. The authors attribute the property to the fact that each attention layer builds its space by interpolating vectors of the previous one (p.487).
concepts.significance: The basis of the 'interpolative database' view: it gives generalization but also hallucination (pp.487-488).
concepts.example: Averaging the vectors for 'king' and 'queen' gives a point near 'monarch' or 'royal'.
concepts.misconception: That interpolation can create genuinely new knowledge. The authors argue (p.488) that it cannot synthesize something fundamentally new.

concepts.name: Cosine similarity / cosine distance
concepts.definition: The cosine of the angle between two vectors, $\frac{\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}}{\|\mathbf{a}\|\|\mathbf{b}\|}$. Cosine distance is 1 minus that value.
concepts.intuition: It measures whether two vectors point the same way, ignoring their length.
concepts.technical: For unit-normalized vectors it equals the dot-product. The page treats 'dot-product' and 'cosine proximity' as interchangeable, which is exact only after normalization.
concepts.significance: The page names cosine distance as the shared distance function for both models.
concepts.misconception: That dot-product and cosine are always the same. A long vector can have a large dot-product while pointing in a fairly different direction.

math.title: The gender vector analogy

variables.meaning: The learned embedding vector of word w
The 'gender vector', an offset approximately shared by many male/female pairs

math.operations: Vector subtraction and addition, followed (implicitly) by a nearest-neighbour search under cosine similarity.
math.purpose: Demonstrates that semantic relations are encoded as directions in the learned space.
math.interpretation: Remove the 'male' component of king, add the 'female' component, and you land near queen. The book writes '='. In practice it means 'the nearest vocabulary vector is'.
math.intuition: The arrows man→woman and king→queen are parallel and of similar length.
math.numerical_example: Toy 2-D vectors (axis 1 = royalty, axis 2 = maleness): king=(0.9, 0.8), man=(0.1, 0.8), woman=(0.1, 0.1), queen=(0.9, 0.1). Then king - man + woman = (0.9-0.1+0.1, 0.8-0.8+0.1) = (0.9, 0.1) = queen exactly. Real 300-d vectors only land *near* queen.

math.title: Cosine proximity used by both models
math.source_text: the dot-product (cosine proximity) … The distance function used to compare tokens is cosine distance in both cases.
math.operations: Dot product normalized by the two lengths.
math.purpose: Measures how aligned two embeddings are. Co-occurring tokens should score near 1.
math.interpretation: 1 means same direction, 0 means orthogonal (unrelated, as one-hot vectors always are, p.433), and -1 means opposite.
math.intuition: It is an angle-based closeness that ignores how long the vectors are.
math.numerical_example: a=(2,1), b=(1,2): a·b=4, ‖a‖=‖b‖=√5, so cos=4/5=0.8 and cosine distance=0.2.

math.title: Attention as similarity-weighted recombination
math.source_text: linearly recombining token embeddings from some prior space, in weighted combinations that give greater importance to tokens that are already “closer” to each other (i.e., that have a higher dot-product)

variables.meaning: Query, key and value projections of the previous-layer token vectors
Attention weight of token j for token i; non-negative and summing to 1 over j
Key/query dimension; dividing by √d keeps scores in a reasonable range
Token i's vector in the new embedding space

math.operations: Dot-product scores, softmax normalization, then a weighted sum.
math.purpose: Formalizes the page's verbal description of attention (the formula itself is given in 15.3.1).
math.interpretation: Higher dot-product gives a larger weight, so the new vector is pulled toward similar tokens. Because the weights are convex, $\mathbf{y}_i$ interpolates the value vectors.
math.intuition: Each token becomes a blend of its most similar neighbours.
math.numerical_example: Scores (q·k/√d) of 2, 1, 0 give weights ≈ 0.665, 0.245, 0.090. With 1-D values 1, 0, -1, the output is 0.665·1 + 0.245·0 + 0.090·(-1) ≈ 0.575, a point between the values, closest to the most similar token's.

deeper.title: Why similarity-weighted averaging pulls close tokens together
deeper.body:
1. Take two tokens A and B whose vectors already have a high dot-product.
2. In attention, A gives B a large weight and B gives A a large weight.
3. A's new vector is roughly A plus a lot of B; B's new vector is roughly B plus a lot of A.
4. Their new vectors are therefore *more* similar than before. Averaging shrinks differences.
5. Tokens with low dot-product barely mix, so they stay apart.
6. Repeat over many layers and training steps, and the geometry increasingly mirrors which tokens co-occur in useful contexts. This is the authors' 'correlation turns into proximity'.

Caveat (not in the book): real Transformers use learned query/key/value projections, residual connections and feedforward layers, so this is a qualitative picture, not a theorem. Pure repeated averaging would eventually collapse all vectors to one point; residual connections and the feedforward layers prevent that.

deeper.title: Word2Vec vs Transformer at a glance
deeper.body:
| | Word2Vec | Transformer |
|---|---|---|
| Units | words | words or subwords |
| Learning signal | predict neighbours / co-occurrence | predict missing or next tokens |
| Mechanism that groups tokens | direct dot-product objective | attention (dot-product-weighted recombination) |
| Embeddings | one static vector per word | a new contextual space per layer |
| Depth | shallow, single layer (p.487) | dozens of stacked blocks |
| Can generate text | no | yes |

The first four rows reflect the page; the depth and generation rows are developed on p.487.

deeper.title: A map analogy for continuity and interpolation
deeper.body: Think of a well-drawn terrain map. **Continuity**: walking a few metres changes the landscape only slightly. **Interpolation**: walking straight from a forest to a beach passes through scrubland, an in-between landscape. A badly drawn map, like a one-hot code, would put every location in its own disconnected cell, so 'halfway between' would mean nothing.

misconceptions.claim: Word2Vec was explicitly trained to solve analogies like king:queen.
misconceptions.correction: The page stresses that the model 'had not been trained for this in any explicit way'. Analogy structure emerged from the co-occurrence objective.

misconceptions.claim: V(king) - V(man) + V(woman) equals V(queen) exactly.
misconceptions.correction: The result is only close to V(queen). It is found by nearest-neighbour search under cosine similarity, and the input words are usually excluded from the search.

misconceptions.claim: Because Transformers are trained to predict words, they have nothing to do with embedding geometry.
misconceptions.correction: The authors' point is that attention, used to predict words, keeps reorganizing token embeddings so that correlations become proximities, the same principle as Word2Vec.

misconceptions.claim: Transformer embeddings are, like Word2Vec, one fixed vector per word.
misconceptions.correction: A Transformer produces a new, context-dependent embedding space at each layer, 'a series of incrementally refined embedding spaces'.

takeaways: Word2Vec turned word co-occurrence into dot-product/cosine proximity, and analogy 'word arithmetic' (the gender vector) emerged without being trained for.
The authors argue that large Transformers share Word2Vec's core: token embeddings, the co-occurrence-to-proximity principle, and cosine comparison.
Attention connects the language-modeling loss to that principle: it recombines token vectors weighted by dot-product closeness, pulling close tokens closer.
A Transformer is a stack of incrementally refined embedding spaces, each built from the previous one.
Attention-built spaces are semantically continuous (small moves mean small changes in meaning) and semantically interpolative (midpoints mean in-between things).
Treat the page's '1,000-10,000 dimensions' figure with caution: Word2Vec typically uses 300 dimensions and RoBERTa base uses 768.

questions.question: According to the page, what is the answer to the question 'How does the language model loss function relate to Word2Vec's objective of maximizing the dot-product between co-occurring tokens?'
questions.explanation: The text says outright: 'The answer is the attention mechanism.' Attention recombines embeddings weighted by dot-product closeness, which pulls co-occurring tokens together. Positional embeddings add word-order information (p.475). Feedforward layers and the output softmax process tokens one at a time and do not mix information across tokens.

questions.question: With toy vectors king=(0.9, 0.8), man=(0.1, 0.8), woman=(0.1, 0.1), compute V(king) - V(man) + V(woman). Then find its cosine similarity to queen=(0.9, 0.1).
questions.explanation: (0.9-0.1+0.1, 0.8-0.8+0.1) = (0.9, 0.1), which is identical to queen, so the cosine is 1. In real embeddings the result is only *near* queen, and queen is chosen as the nearest neighbour.

questions.question: Name the four similarities the authors list between Word2Vec and Transformers.
questions.answer: Both embed tokens (words or subwords) in a vector space; both learn the space on the principle that co-occurring tokens end up close; both compare tokens with cosine distance; both use embedding vectors of similar dimensionality.
questions.explanation: These come straight from the 'Both models seek to embed tokens…' paragraph. Note that the stated range of 1,000-10,000 dimensions is inaccurate for Word2Vec (usually 300).

questions.question: Why would giving more weight to tokens that already have a higher dot-product tend to pull those tokens even closer together?
questions.answer: Each token's new vector is a weighted average dominated by its similar neighbours. When two similar tokens each mix in a large share of the other, their new vectors are more alike than before, while dissimilar tokens barely mix.
questions.explanation: Averaging reduces differences between the things averaged. With dot-product weights, the averaging is concentrated among already-similar tokens, so correlation becomes proximity, as the page claims.

questions.question: Which statement describes 'semantically interpolative' as defined on the page?
options: Small moves in the space change meaning only slightly
The midpoint between two embeddings represents an intermediate meaning
Each token has exactly one fixed vector
Distances are measured with L2 rather than cosine
questions.answer: The midpoint between two embeddings represents an intermediate meaning
questions.explanation: The second bullet defines interpolation as the intermediate point producing an 'intermediate meaning'. The first option is semantic continuity, the other property. Fixed vectors describe Word2Vec, not Transformer layers. The page names cosine, not L2.

questions.question: In what sense is a Transformer 'a series of incrementally refined embedding spaces'?
questions.answer: Each attention block takes the previous layer's token vectors and outputs new vectors built by recombining them, so every layer defines a new, more contextual embedding space for the next layer.
questions.explanation: This paraphrases the page's final sentence about attention. Unlike Word2Vec's single static table, the representation of each token changes layer by layer.

questions.question: Can you explain to a friend, without equations, why Word2Vec's 'gender vector' was surprising and how it foreshadows what the authors say about Transformers?
questions.answer: Self-assessment: it was surprising because the model was only trained on co-occurrence, yet one consistent direction encoded gender for many word pairs. It foreshadows the claim that Transformers learn far richer 'functions' (vector programs, p.487) as a by-product of organizing tokens in space.
questions.explanation: If you can link 'emergent direction' to 'emergent function', you have the thread that runs from this page to p.487.
